title: PlantBGC: Transformer for Plant BGC Discovery via Label-Free Domain Adaptation and Weak Supervision
summary: Plant biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) encode specialized-metabolite pathways, yet curated plant BGC labels remain scarce, hindering supervised discovery at genome scale. Existing plant BGC mining tools are largely signature- and rule-driven and do not fully leverage recent advances in contextual representation learning for modeling long-range domain context and controlling false positives under strong domain shift. We seek an AI-assisted workflow that narrows experimental search space by transferring supervision from well-annotated microbial BGCs to plant genomes. We present PlantBGC, representing genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences and learning BGC-likeness with an encoder-only Transformer trained on MIBiG microbial BGCs and adapted to plants via label-free masked language modeling. On microbial benchmarks, PlantBGC achieves token-level AUC = 0.988 (10-fold CV) and 0.979 (leave-class-out). On plants, adaptation improves known-BGC recovery on n = 34 curated loci under strict 100% coverage, increasing recovery from 29.4% to 67.6% and indicating more complete boundaries. GO/KEGG-derived weak supervision reduces proxy primary-like ratio by 48.40% (GO) and 45.20% (KEGG), with consistent per-species reductions (paired Wilcoxon p = 1.53e-5). Compared to plantiSMASH, PlantBGC yields more compact loci on matched regions (median length ratio = 0.278; 93.8% of pairs are shorter).

AI.tldr: PlantBGC is an encoder-only Transformer that represents plant genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences, transferring supervision from microbial BGCs (MIBiG) to plants via label-free masked language modeling, improving curated BGC recovery from 29.4% to 67.6% and producing more compact loci than plantiSMASH.
AI.motivation: Curated plant BGC labels are scarce, hindering supervised genome-scale discovery. Existing plant BGC tools are signature- and rule-driven and do not leverage contextual representation learning for long-range domain modeling or control false positives under domain shift. An AI-assisted workflow is needed to narrow experimental search space by transferring supervision from annotated microbial BGCs.
AI.method: PlantBGC represents genomes as ordered Pfam-domain sequences and learns BGC-likeness using an encoder-only Transformer pretrained on MIBiG microbial BGCs, then adapts to plants via label-free masked language modeling. Weak supervision from GO/KEGG annotations further refines predictions.
AI.result: Token-level AUC = 0.988 (10-fold CV) and 0.979 (leave-class-out) on microbial benchmarks. On plants, adaptation raises strict 100%-coverage BGC recovery from 29.4% to 67.6%. GO/KEGG weak supervision reduces proxy primary-like ratio by 48.40% (GO) and 45.20% (KEGG) with consistent per-species reductions (Wilcoxon p=1.53e-5). PlantBGC yields more compact loci (median length ratio=0.278; 93.8% shorter) than plantiSMASH.
AI.conclusion: Transfer learning from microbial BGCs combined with masked language model adaptation enables effective plant BGC discovery, improving recovery rates and prediction specificity while yielding more precise locus boundaries than existing rule-based tools.

title: IndelFreeAligner: A Streaming Aligner for Comprehensive Gapless Alignment Against Terabase-Scale References
summary: The comparison of short sequences to massive reference databases is a cornerstone of modern genomics, but it presents a significant scalability challenge. Traditional alignment tools rely on time- and memory-intensive pre-indexing of the reference, creating a substantial bottleneck for applications involving small query sets against terabase-scale data, such as CRISPR spacer analysis. Here we present IndelFreeAligner, a streaming, indel-free alignment tool that eliminates the preprocessing bottleneck. It operates in two modes: an indexed mode for larger query sets and a brute-force mode for maximum speed on small query sets. By processing reference sequences on-the-fly, IndelFreeAligner supports user-specified mismatch thresholds up to the full query length and maintains memory usage independent of total reference size. A novel MinHitsCalculator component uses Monte Carlo simulation to determine adaptive seed-hit thresholds for indexed mode. Benchmarks against Bowtie1 and BLAST+ demonstrate that IndelFreeAligner aligns a single query against a 4 Gbp reference in 1.7 seconds versus 17 minutes for Bowtie1 (including index construction at optimal thread count), a 607-fold speedup. Against RefSeq Bacteria (560 GB compressed), IndelFreeAligner completes a 10-query search in 12 minutes using 8 GB of RAM, while BLAST+ requires 3 hours and 17 minutes to build its database alone and 506 GB of RAM to query it. Indexed mode achieves 0% false negatives through 4 substitutions (99.84-99.90% mapped at 8-16); brute-force mode is exhaustive by design. IndelFreeAligner provides a scalable and efficient solution for alignment tasks that were previously computationally prohibitive. It is distributed open-source as part of BBTools (Bushnell, 2014).

AI.tldr: IndelFreeAligner is a streaming, indel-free alignment tool that eliminates the preprocessing/indexing bottleneck of traditional aligners. It processes references on-the-fly, supports user-specified mismatch thresholds, and uses Monte Carlo simulation to set adaptive seed-hit thresholds in indexed mode. It achieves a 607-fold speedup over Bowtie1 on single-query alignments and vastly outperforms BLAST+ on terabase-scale references.
AI.motivation: Traditional alignment tools require time- and memory-intensive pre-indexing of reference databases, which creates a substantial bottleneck for applications with small query sets against terabase-scale data (e.g., CRISPR spacer analysis).
AI.method: IndelFreeAligner operates in two modes: an indexed mode for larger query sets and a brute-force mode for maximum speed on small query sets. It streams reference sequences on-the-fly, supports mismatch thresholds up to the full query length, and maintains memory usage independent of reference size. A MinHitsCalculator component uses Monte Carlo simulation to determine adaptive seed-hit thresholds for indexed mode.
AI.result: Aligns a single query against a 4 Gbp reference in 1.7 seconds versus 17 minutes for Bowtie1 (607-fold speedup). Against RefSeq Bacteria (560 GB compressed), completes a 10-query search in 12 minutes using 8 GB RAM, while BLAST+ requires 3h17m just to build its database and 506 GB RAM to query. Indexed mode achieves 0% false negatives through 4 substitutions.
AI.conclusion: IndelFreeAligner provides a scalable and efficient solution for alignment tasks that were previously computationally prohibitive, and is distributed open-source as part of BBTools.

title: Identifying common backbones of interactions underlying food webs via non-deterministic alignments
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICASSP 2026
summary: Climate change reshapes food webs by altering species distributions and interactions, making it essential to identify structural backbones of interactions that persist across ecosystems. Deterministic alignment methods are computationally slow and restricted to one-to-one correspondences. We introduce a scalable, non-deterministic alignment framework inspired by optimal transport that captures overlapping species roles via many-to-many mappings. Framed via motif-role profiles as a Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem, our method is both efficient and interpretable. We apply the proposed method to a large continental-scale data set of 129 mammal food webs in Sub-Saharan Africa. Pairwise alignments are identified, and we uncover robust backbones with greater connectivity and transitivity than those expected under null models. The proposed approach provides a formal, reproducible tool for forecasting ecosystem reorganization and conservation efforts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a scalable, non-deterministic framework for aligning food webs across ecosystems using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport and motif-role profiles, enabling many-to-many species mappings. Applied to 129 mammal food webs in Sub-Saharan Africa, it reveals robust structural backbones with higher connectivity and transitivity than null models, offering a tool for ecosystem forecasting and conservation.
AI.motivation: Climate change alters species distributions and interactions, making it crucial to identify structural backbones of food-web interactions that persist across ecosystems. Existing deterministic alignment methods are computationally slow and limited to one-to-one correspondences, which fail to capture overlapping species roles across ecosystems.
AI.method: The method frames food-web alignment as a Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport problem using motif-role profiles, allowing scalable, non-deterministic many-to-many mappings between species across ecosystems. It is applied to a large continental-scale dataset of 129 mammal food webs in Sub-Saharan Africa to identify pairwise alignments.
AI.result: The method uncovers robust structural backbones across the 129 mammal food webs that exhibit greater connectivity and transitivity than expected under null models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the scalable alignment framework on large-scale ecological data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a formal, interpretable, and reproducible tool for forecasting ecosystem reorganization under climate change, with direct applications to conservation planning and management.

title: The evolution of cooperation under imperfect phenotypic recognition
summary: Phenotypic similarity is a classical mechanism for the evolution of cooperation. Most existing models assume a binary rule in which individuals cooperate only with others of the same phenotype. This assumption is biologically restrictive, since recognition and discrimination are often gradual rather than all-or-nothing. In this paper, we extend the multidimensional phenotype-space model of cooperation by allowing the probability of helping to decline with phenotypic distance. In a large population under weak selection with mutation in both strategy and phenotype, we derive a generalized threshold for selection to favor the abundance of cooperation and express it using a new Laplace-type transform. We show that this threshold decreases strictly as discrimination becomes sharper, meaning that exact phenotype matching is the most favorable limit within this family of recognition rules. We also show that the threshold decreases strictly with phenotype-space dimension, meaning that higher-dimensional phenotype spaces promote cooperation even when recognition is imperfect. Our asymptotic analysis further shows that low phenotype mutations strongly inhibit cooperation, whereas sufficiently high phenotype mutations drive the threshold toward its minimal value. However, high strategy mutation makes cooperation harder to maintain.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the multidimensional phenotype-space model of cooperation by replacing binary phenotype matching with gradual recognition, where the probability of helping declines continuously with phenotypic distance. The authors derive a generalized selection threshold using a Laplace-type transform and show that sharper discrimination, higher phenotype-space dimensionality, and higher phenotype mutation rates all promote cooperation, while higher strategy mutation rates hinder it.
AI.motivation: Existing models of phenotype-based cooperation assume an all-or-nothing matching rule, which is biologically unrealistic since recognition and discrimination are typically gradual. The authors aim to relax this restrictive assumption to better reflect natural systems.
AI.method: The authors extend the multidimensional phenotype-space model by allowing the probability of helping to decline continuously with phenotypic distance. They analyze a large population under weak selection with mutation in both strategy and phenotype, deriving a generalized threshold condition for cooperation to be favored. The threshold is expressed using a new Laplace-type transform, and they perform asymptotic analyses of phenotype and strategy mutation rates.
AI.result: (1) The selection threshold decreases strictly as discrimination becomes sharper, making exact matching the most favorable limit. (2) The threshold decreases with phenotype-space dimension, so higher-dimensional spaces promote cooperation even with imperfect recognition. (3) Low phenotype mutation strongly inhibits cooperation, while sufficiently high phenotype mutation pushes the threshold to its minimum. (4) High strategy mutation makes cooperation harder to maintain.
AI.conclusion: Gradual, distance-based recognition rules preserve the qualitative predictions of the binary matching model but add important nuance: cooperation is promoted by sharper discrimination, higher phenotype dimensionality, and higher phenotypic mutation, though it is hindered by fast strategy mutation.

title: Evolutionary adaptation through bet-hedging in finite populations under fluctuating environments
summary: Natural populations evolve under fluctuating environments and limited resources, yet it is unclear how these factors jointly shape adaptation. Here, we introduce a minimal stochastic model of a population undergoing a birth-death process in a randomly switching environment, where individuals inherit phenotypic strategies that determine the distribution of phenotypes across generations. First, we confirm that environmental variability can favor phenotypic diversity (bet-hedging), and that the strategy maximizing the average growth rate generally differs from the one minimizing extinction risk. We then demonstrate that evolution drives populations toward strategies that balance these competing objectives. Furthermore, we show that population size modulates this evolutionary outcome: large populations converge to the growth-maximizing strategy, whereas smaller ones evolve toward more resilient strategies. Finally, we provide a simple heuristic approximation that captures these results, clarifying the interplay between growth, extinction, and mutation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a minimal stochastic model of populations undergoing birth-death processes in randomly switching environments, showing that evolution balances growth maximization against extinction risk minimization, and that population size modulates which strategy dominates.
AI.motivation: Natural populations evolve under both fluctuating environments and limited resources, but the joint effect of these factors on adaptation remains unclear.
AI.method: A minimal stochastic birth-death model in a randomly switching environment, where individuals inherit phenotypic strategies determining phenotype distributions across generations.
AI.result: Environmental variability favors bet-hedging; growth-maximizing and extinction-minimizing strategies differ; evolution balances these objectives; large populations converge to growth-maximizing strategies while smaller populations evolve toward more resilient ones; a simple heuristic captures these results.
AI.conclusion: Population size modulates evolutionary outcomes, with a trade-off between growth and extinction shaping adaptation in fluctuating environments.

title: A data-driven stage-structured host-parasitoid model for optimizing Trichogramma interventions against soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) outbreaks
summary: The soybean pod borer (Leguminivora glycinivorella) poses a severe threat to global soybean production.In this study, we developed a stage-structured host-parasitoid dynamic model that explicitly couples the holometabolous life cycle of the pest with the obligate egg-parasitism mechanism of Trichogramma wasps. Utilizing field monitoring data from Changchun, Jilin Province, key biological parameters were rigorously estimated via the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method.This calibration facilitated the establishment of a precise Economic Injury Level ($Q_{EIL}$) of 0.0389 individuals/$m^2$, based solely on the destructive larval stage. Through theoretical and numerical analyses of different intervention scenarios, we identified an optimal continuous release rate ($C^* = 2.645$) that efficiently suppresses the outbreak without causing wasteful parasitoid accumulation. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that a 5-day impulsive release interval provides the optimal balance between strict pest suppression and field operational costs. This study bridges the gap between theoretical population dynamics and applied agricultural management, providing a directly applicable mathematical decision-making tool for the precise biological control of crop pests.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a stage-structured host-parasitoid model coupling the soybean pod borer's holometabolous life cycle with Trichogramma wasp egg parasitism, calibrates it with field data via MCMC, establishes a precise Economic Injury Level (0.0389 individuals/m²), and identifies an optimal continuous release rate (C*=2.645) and a 5-day impulsive release interval for efficient biological pest control.
AI.motivation: The soybean pod borer is a severe threat to global soybean production, and effective biological control strategies are needed. The study aims to bridge theoretical population dynamics with applied agricultural management by developing a decision-making tool for precise biological control.
AI.method: The authors developed a stage-structured host-parasitoid dynamic model explicitly coupling the holometabolous life cycle of the pest with the obligate egg-parasitism mechanism of Trichogramma wasps. Key biological parameters were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) from field monitoring data in Changchun, Jilin Province. Theoretical and numerical analyses of different intervention scenarios were conducted.
AI.result: The model established a precise Economic Injury Level (EIL) of 0.0389 individuals/m² based on the destructive larval stage. An optimal continuous release rate (C*=2.645) was identified that suppresses outbreaks without wasteful parasitoid accumulation, and a 5-day impulsive release interval provides the optimal balance between pest suppression and field operational costs.
AI.conclusion: The study bridges theoretical population dynamics and applied agricultural management, providing a directly applicable mathematical decision-making tool for the precise biological control of crop pests through optimized Trichogramma wasp release strategies.

title: Stimulus-Evoked Network Dynamics in Human Cortical Organoids: From a Graph-Computational Framework to Repeated-Stimulation Depression
summary: Human cortical organoids provide an experimentally accessible model of early neural circuit formation, yet whether their activity reflects structured information processing rather than spontaneous synchronization is unclear. We developed a graph-computational framework to quantify stimulus-evoked propagation. This includes stimulus-conditioned functional graphs, a graph-constrained dynamical (graph-neural-network) model used as a system-identification tool, a biological message-passing principle bounding integration depth by observable propagation depth, and a suite of graph-level metrics. We carried this program out in full on longitudinal HD-MEA recordings from three organoids. Once the true acquisition sampling rate and stimulus timing were recovered, the evoked response proved to be a fast, near-synchronous network burst with no measurable outward propagation (peak-latency vs. distance slope = 0). The propagation/integration-depth metrics (Deff ,reachability index, dmax) therefore do not apply, and per-day connectivity graphs were not reliably estimable at the available trial count, a negative result with methodological consequences for applying such metrics to organoid data. Reframing around synchrony, response-population size and shared variability revealed a control-validated phenomenon, i.e., repeated daily stimulation progressively depressed and spatially contracted the evoked response. That repeated stimulation reshapes organoid networks is established, but longitudinal designs in which every preparation is stimulated cannot separate this from developmental maturation. We break that confound with a developmentally-matched, stimulation-naive control, where at day 7, an organoid receiving its first-ever stimulation engaged 93% of the array, whereas organoids with five prior sessions engaged 10%.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a graph-computational framework to analyze stimulus-evoked activity in human cortical organoids, but finds that responses are fast, near-synchronous bursts with no outward propagation. Instead, the key finding is that repeated daily stimulation progressively depresses and spatially contracts evoked responses (93% array engagement at first stimulation vs. 10% after five prior sessions), validated with a developmentally-matched, stimulation-naive control.
AI.motivation: To determine whether stimulus-evoked activity in human cortical organoids reflects structured information processing (propagation) rather than mere spontaneous synchronization, and to properly assess the applicability of graph-based integration metrics to organoid data.
AI.method: Developed a graph-computational framework including stimulus-conditioned functional graphs, a graph-neural-network dynamical model for system identification, a biological message-passing principle, and graph-level metrics. Applied on longitudinal HD-MEA recordings from three organoids, with a developmentally-matched stimulation-naive control to break the confound between repeated stimulation and developmental maturation.
AI.result: Evoked responses were fast, near-synchronous network bursts with zero propagation slope, making propagation/integration-depth metrics inapplicable. Connectivity graphs were not reliably estimable at available trial counts. Instead, repeated daily stimulation progressively depressed and spatially contracted evoked responses: a naive organoid engaged 93% of the array on first stimulation vs. 10% for organoids with five prior sessions.
AI.conclusion: Repeated stimulation itself reshapes organoid network responsivity (depression and spatial contraction), independent of developmental maturation. Graph-information-processing metrics are not applicable to organoid data showing synchronous-burst dynamics, and methodological caution is needed when applying such frameworks.

title: Hash Chemistry: Minimal Models for Evolutionary Growth of Complexity
summary: Hash Chemistry is a family of minimalistic evolutionary models in which a deterministic hash function assigns a scalar score to entities of arbitrary size, opening a combinatorially vast possibility space (a ``cardinality leap''). Since its introduction, the idea has been realized in several settings, from the original spatial formulation to a fast non-spatial variant and then to structural cellular models. Here we review the Hash Chemistry family as a coherent modeling framework and use it to explore how minimal systems can demonstrate the mechanisms behind multiscale open-ended evolutionary dynamics. The most recent model, Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC), successfully demonstrated multiscale ecological interaction/adaptation and complexity growth of replicators in a computationally efficient manner. In this study, we first extend SCHC to incorporate spatial locality and dyadicity of competitive interactions among replicating structures. We show this extension substantially enhances SCHC's evolutionary dynamics. Furthermore, we explore SCHC in a significantly larger spatial domain using a GPU-accelerated implementation. We show that the size of the space acts as a control parameter for a stochastic, nucleation-like transition between a compact-replicator regime and a runaway size-dominance regime, and we separate the responsible mechanism into a non-spatial, size-biased sampling feedback and a finite-size spatial effect. Altogether, these results illustrate the rich potential of Hash Chemistry as a minimal, mechanistically transparent testbed for studying open-ended evolution across scales.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the Hash Chemistry family of minimalistic evolutionary models and extends the most recent variant, Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC), by incorporating spatial locality and dyadicity of competitive interactions. The extension enhances evolutionary dynamics, and using GPU-accelerated large-scale simulations, the authors discover a stochastic nucleation-like transition between a compact-replicator regime and a runaway size-dominance regime, driven by size-biased sampling feedback and finite-size spatial effects. Hash Chemistry is positioned as a mechanistically transparent testbed for open-ended evolution.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate how minimal systems can reveal the mechanisms behind multiscale open-ended evolutionary dynamics, and to push the Hash Chemistry framework toward richer, more realistic evolutionary behavior by adding spatial structure.
AI.method: The authors extend Structural Cellular Hash Chemistry (SCHC) to include spatial locality and dyadicity of competitive interactions among replicating structures. They implement GPU-accelerated simulations to explore much larger spatial domains than previously possible.
AI.result: The spatial extension substantially enhances SCHC's evolutionary dynamics. In large-scale simulations, a stochastic nucleation-like transition emerges between a compact-replicator regime and a runaway size-dominance regime. The mechanism is decomposed into (1) a non-spatial, size-biased sampling feedback and (2) a finite-size spatial effect.
AI.conclusion: Hash Chemistry is a rich, minimal, and mechanistically transparent framework for studying open-ended evolution across scales, with the spatial extension of SCHC offering new insights into regime transitions and evolutionary dynamics.

title: Causal Architecture Dynamics Prior to Arrival of Self-replicators in a Model of Catalytic Networks Relevant to Origin-of-Life
summary: Agents that exert causal power in the world are thought to be the product of selection among diverse replicators; what is the causal structure of a medium before replicators appear, and evolution takes hold? We studied information-theoretic dynamics of the popular GARD model that captures several dynamics thought to be important at life's origin and found that causal emergence predicted the initial appearance of self-replication. Moreover, interventions that drove causal emergence up increased the longevity of self-replicators, while interventions that drove causal emergence down decreased the abundance of these self-replicators, suggesting causal emergence as a functional control knob. Thus, progressive increases in integrated causality are detectable in active media before evolutionary dynamics begin to operate, which may have implications for the origin of life across highly diverse scenarios and for understanding the forces driving the rise in causal power observed in the biosphere on Earth.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the information-theoretic dynamics of the GARD model (a popular model of life's origin) and finds that causal emergence predicts the initial appearance of self-replication before traditional evolutionary dynamics take hold. Interventions that increased causal emergence enhanced replicator longevity, while decreasing it reduced replicator abundance, suggesting causal emergence acts as a functional control knob for the onset of self-replication.
AI.motivation: To understand the causal structure of a medium before replicators appear and evolution takes hold, asking what forces drive the initial rise in causal power in the biosphere.
AI.method: The authors analyzed information-theoretic dynamics of the GARD (Graded Autocatalysis Replication Domain) model, measuring causal emergence in the system and performing intervention experiments that drove causal emergence up or down to test its effects on self-replicator longevity and abundance.
AI.result: Causal emergence predicted the initial appearance of self-replication. Increasing causal emergence increased self-replicator longevity, while decreasing it reduced self-replicator abundance.
AI.conclusion: Progressive increases in integrated causality are detectable in active media before evolutionary dynamics begin, suggesting causal emergence as a precursor and potential driver of self-replication, with implications for the origin of life across diverse scenarios.

title: Multi-scale measures of time-varying epidemic spread on human mobility networks
summary: Human movement drives the spatial spread and persistence of many infectious diseases, yet existing theory and real-time operational tools for inferring the instantaneous reproduction number R(t) often assume static and/or homogeneously mixing populations and cannot describe how individuals generate and acquire infections heterogeneously based on their movement patterns within a day. Renewal equations underpin many such popular estimators of R(t), and here, we develop a network-based modelling framework from which we derive new mechanism-led renewal equations and control indicators for outbreaks of infectious diseases. These equations directly integrate within-day human movement to rigorously define a family of instantaneous reproduction numbers; inward, outward, and type R(t) for individual locations, R(t) between locations, R(t) at meeting locations, and R(t) for the entire mobility network. These quantities correct for the unsuitability of existing location-specific R(t) estimators that operate in closed, static populations. Applying our framework to epidemics on diverse types of networks alongside mobile phone data, we demonstrate how our new framework's outputs provide new, multi-scale control indicators at the network, location, and transmission corridor scales, and can be used to design targeted disease control interventions including the strength, type, and length of intervention required across space and time. We capture the biasing effects of different existing ways to measure location-specific and network-level transmission potential without capturing within-day human movements. This generalisable framework redefines reproduction numbers in real-world outbreaks that are shaped by individuals moving across connected locations, enabling more spatially and temporally precise interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a network-based modeling framework that incorporates within-day human movement into renewal equations, deriving a family of location-specific and network-level instantaneous reproduction numbers (R(t)) that correct for biases in existing estimators that assume static, homogeneously mixing populations.
AI.motivation: Existing theories and tools for estimating the instantaneous reproduction number R(t) assume static and/or homogeneously mixing populations, failing to account for how within-day human movement drives heterogeneous infection generation and acquisition across connected locations.
AI.method: The authors develop a network-based modeling framework from which they derive new mechanism-led renewal equations that integrate within-day human movement, defining a family of instantaneous reproduction numbers: inward, outward, and type R(t) for individual locations, R(t) between locations, R(t) at meeting locations, and network-level R(t).
AI.result: Applying the framework to diverse network types and mobile phone data, the authors demonstrate new multi-scale control indicators at network, location, and transmission corridor scales, enable targeted intervention design (strength, type, length), and quantify biasing effects of existing location-specific and network-level estimators that ignore within-day movement.
AI.conclusion: This generalizable framework redefines reproduction numbers for real-world outbreaks shaped by human movement across connected locations, enabling more spatially and temporally precise disease control interventions.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction, supporting variable-length sequences up to 30s, arbitrary channel configurations and locations, and partial temporal reconstruction, matching or exceeding its predecessor ZUNA1 while outperforming standard methods like spherical spline interpolation. Released open source under Apache 2.0.
AI.motivation: To provide a more flexible EEG reconstruction model that can handle diverse real-world scenarios including variable-length sequences, arbitrary scalp locations, and partial temporal gaps, while maintaining or improving performance over existing methods.
AI.method: A 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder architecture designed for flexible EEG signal reconstruction with support for variable sequence lengths (up to 30s), arbitrary channel counts and scalp positions, and selective temporal interval reconstruction within channels.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with ZUNA1 while being significantly more flexible, and substantially outperforms standard methods such as spherical spline interpolation used in MNE.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 provides a flexible, high-performing open-source solution for EEG reconstruction tasks, expanding the practical applicability of diffusion-based EEG reconstruction.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
summary: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Rational Mentalizing model that explains how humans decide between social learning (observing others) and non-social learning (direct exploration), showing the model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between these strategies in a novel game.
AI.motivation: Humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning despite its cognitive and time costs, raising the question of how people balance social and non-social learning strategies.
AI.method: The Rational Mentalizing model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goals and the informativeness of their future actions, then weighs this against the utility of non-social learning. The model is tested using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment.
AI.result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social and non-social learning strategies in the game.
AI.conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind in the service of utility maximization.

title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
summary: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

AI.tldr: KAISEN is a five-phase clinical risk model audit pipeline (subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, drift monitoring) stress-tested to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes, and 3 intersections. Four key findings emerge: (i) significance tracking improves dramatically when EOD is standardized by minimum detectable effect; (ii) per-group threshold optimization reliably reduces disparity while Platt scaling behaves randomly on EOD; (iii) mechanism diagnostics succeed on controlled cases but silently fail under proxy misspecification; (iv) CUSUM drift detection is cohort-seed-dependent and thresholds fail to transfer.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk models show strong aggregate performance but disparate error rates across subgroups. While audit pipelines exist to catch disparities, their individual components are rarely stress-tested, leaving unclear which parts can be trusted and under what conditions.
AI.method: The authors build KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline, and evaluate each component to the point of failure using a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth: 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and 3 prespecified intersections. Statistical analyses include rank correlations, paired comparisons of mitigation strategies, controlled mechanism diagnostic tests, and CUSUM drift monitoring across cohort seeds.
AI.result: (i) Significance vs. EOD rank correlation is rho=0.56, rising to 0.78 when EOD is standardized by minimum detectable effect. (ii) Threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48/48 runs (delta=-0.285, CI [-0.313,-0.252]) while Platt scaling improves only 19/48 runs with mean effect near zero. (iii) Mechanism diagnostic classifies 144/144 controlled cases but 0/48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no failure signal. (iv) All 27 false alarms and 7/8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p=0.002), showing threshold non-transferability.
AI.conclusion: Audit pipelines can perform well on some components while silently failing on others. The authors recommend reporting variance rather than averages (e.g., for mitigations like Platt scaling), standardizing disparity metrics by minimum detectable effect, and cautioning that mechanism diagnostics and drift thresholds may not transfer across cohorts. All results are synthetic and do not establish clinical validity; code and artifacts are publicly released for reproducibility.
